Next, we post-trained the model using Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR), with a difficulty-aware loop curriculum that routes harder prompts to deeper loops. Increasing the loop count improves accuracy, with the largest gains on coding, agentic, and long-context benchmarks. With two or more loops, Dory1.0-4B outperforms larger models such as Qwen3.5-9B, Gemma 4 12B, and Gemma 4 26B-A4B on average across 12 benchmarks. Looping also makes Dory1.0-4B more token-efficient on agentic benchmarks: with four loops, it generates 1.3-2.5x fewer tokens than with one loop, as the extra computation is spent in latent space rather than on longer outputs. To reduce memory during looping, Dory1.0-4B caches keys and values only from the last loop, keeping its KV-cache footprint equal to that of a non-looped model at any loop count while retaining most of the accuracy gains. We open-source the BF16, MXFP8, NVFP4, and GGUF quantized checkpoints.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Breast Cancer Diagnosis, Treatment, and Perioperative Management: A Systematic Review of Current Applications and Future Perspectives.
abstract: Background: Breast cancer is the most frequently diagnosed malignancy in women globally, accounting for approximately 2.30 million new cases and 666,103 deaths in 2022. Artificial intelligence technologies including machine learning, deep learning, radiomics, and natural language processing have been widely applied across the breast cancer care continuum. However, no systematic review restricted to primary studies with patient-level or image-level data has synthesized evidence spanning all clinical domains simultaneously. Objectives: To evaluate the performance, methodological quality, and clinical relevance of artificial intelligence primary studies across screening and diagnostic imaging, digital pathology, radiomics, perioperative management, prognostic prediction, and natural language processing in breast cancer. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were searched from January 2015 to May 2026. Eligibility was restricted to original primary research reporting patient-level or image-level data; secondary syntheses were explicitly excluded. Risk of bias was assessed using QUADAS-2 and PROBAST. Reporting followed PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Results: Of 5,275 identified records, 17 primary studies met eligibility criteria. In screening mammography (seven studies; n = 7,540 to 144,231 examinations), deep learning achieved area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) values of 0.876 to 0.939; a randomised trial in 80,033 women demonstrated non-inferiority to double reading with a 44.3% reduction in radiologist workload. In digital pathology (five studies; 270 to 44,732 whole-slide images), deep learning achieved AUC 0.985 to 0.994, exceeding unassisted pathologist performance in lymph node metastasis detection. Magnetic resonance imaging radiomics predicted pathological complete response in HER2-positive breast cancer with AUC 0.80. No breast cancer-specific perioperative primary study met the eligibility criteria. Deep survival networks achieved concordance index 0.626 versus 0.612 for Cox regression in breast cancer cohorts. Natural language processing identified metastatic recurrence in breast cancer clinical records with sensitivity 83% and specificity 73%. Risk of bias was low to moderate for imaging and pathology studies and high for small sample radiomics studies. Density-stratified performance was reported by only two imaging studies, and receptor status prediction from haematoxylin and eosin staining had not been validated as a safe alternative to immunohistochemistry. Conclusions: Artificial intelligence demonstrated clinically meaningful performance across the five domains with eligible primary studies. Breast cancer-specific perioperative and intensive care primary studies were absent, representing the largest evidence gap. External validation, demographic diversity, and prospective clinical integration evidence remained the most consistently identified limitations. Prediction of molecular receptor status without immunohistochemistry requires rigorous prospective safety validation before it can complement standard testing.

title: Necessity–Uncertainty Theory of Information: A Conceptual Framework
abstract: Abstract: Information is often defined as the reduction of uncertainty. This paper argues that uncertainty alone does not fully explain the emergence or value of information. Necessity—the contextual demand to resolve uncertainty—must also be considered. By combining these two dimensions, we propose a simple formula: \[I = N \cdot U\] Here, \(U\) represents uncertainty measured through Shannon entropy, while \(N\) reflects the situational need for information on a scale from 0 to 1. The framework suggests that information arises, and matters, only when uncertainty exists and necessity requires resolution. Examples from communication, decision-making, and knowledge acquisition illustrate the theory’s relevance and practical scope. This framework extends Shannon’s theory by adding a human-centered dimension. It bridges mathematical information theory with epistemology and decision sciences. Everyday interactions—such as tutoring, communication, or decision-making—provide living evidence of the theory. Information is not merely an abstract reduction of entropy; it is the synthesis of uncertainty and necessity within real contexts of human inquiry. At the time of this publication, successful digital-signature generation and public-key verification for this work had not been established. Therefore, SIC256v1 is not claimed here as verified cryptographic proof of authorship, identity, or document integrity. Authorship linked to ORCID iD: https://orcid.org/0009-0008-6637-6752

title: Deep Learning for Sequential Decision Making Under Uncertainty: Foundations, Frameworks, and Frontiers
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is moving increasingly beyond prediction to support decisions in complex, uncertain, and dynamic environments. This shift creates a natural intersection with operations research and management sciences (OR/MS), which have long offered conceptual and methodological foundations for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. At the same time, recent advances in deep learning, including feedforward neural networks, LSTMs, transformers, and deep reinforcement learning, have expanded the scope of data-driven modeling and opened new possibilities for large-scale decision systems. This tutorial presents an OR/MS-centered perspective on deep learning for sequential decision-making under uncertainty. Its central premise is that deep learning is valuable not as a replacement for optimization, but as a complement to it. Deep learning brings adaptability and scalable approximation, whereas OR/MS provides the structural rigor needed to represent constraints, recourse, and uncertainty. The tutorial reviews key decision-making foundations, connects them to the major neural architectures in modern AI, and discusses leading approaches to integrating learning and optimization. It also highlights emerging impact in domains such as supply chains, healthcare and epidemic response, agriculture, energy, and autonomous operations. More broadly, it frames these developments as part of a wider transition from predictive AI toward decision-capable AI and highlights the role of OR/MS in shaping the next generation of integrated learning–optimization systems.

title: Accelerating noisy variational quantum algorithms with physics-informed denoising networks
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms are promising for near-term quantum computing, but are severely limited by hardware noise and the substantial circuit overhead required for error mitigation methods such as Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE). We propose a Physics-Informed Denoising Network (PIDN) that reduces the cost of ZNE by learning a surrogate model of its optimization dynamics. By viewing the variational update as a trajectory in the parameter space, PIDN is trained to reproduce ZNE-mitigated expectation values and gradient directions while incorporating a physics-informed loss that preserves the gradient descent dynamics. Once trained, PIDN replaces repeated multi-noise evaluations with denoised expectation and gradient estimation directly from the current noisy observation and the historical trajectory, significantly reducing circuit executions. We benchmark the approach on the quantum approximate optimization algorithm for 3-regular graphs, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, and transverse-field Ising models, as well as the variational quantum eigensolver for LiH, BeH$_2$ and H$_2$O. Across all tasks, PIDN attains performance comparable to ZNE, while reducing the number of circuit executions by a factor of approximately 4 to 6. Gradient cosine similarity with ZNE remains above 0.95 throughout training. Robustness analysis shows that PIDN fails only when ZNE itself becomes unreliable, and ablation studies confirm the necessity of the physics-informed loss for maintaining directional consistency. We further find that PIDN tracks optimization dynamics most accurately when the effective loss landscape retains strong low-frequency structure. These results establish PIDN as a scalable, resource-efficient strategy for noise-resilient variational optimization in the noisy intermediate-scale quantum regime.

title: Unconditional authentication in quantum key distribution via hybrid entangled physical unclonable functions
abstract: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) enables Information-Theoretically Secure (ITS) key exchange, robust even against future quantum computing threats. However, a fundamental limitation of QKD is the requirement for an authenticated classical channel, which necessitates a pre-shared secret key. In this work, we address this challenge by adopting a Hybrid Entangled Physical Unclonable Function (PUF) protocol for authentication. We demonstrate that this PUF-based method generates an ITS initial key under minimal explicit hardware assumptions. This approach allows us to experimentally perform a fully ITS-authenticated entanglement-based QKD protocol that relies solely on such assumptions, effectively eliminating the need for pre-shared secrets. This represents a significant step towards the practical realization of quantum network protocols using lightweight, readily available hardware assumptions, without weakening security guarantees.

title: Multi-dimensional hierarchical temporal alignment for improved temporal commonsense reasoning in large language models
abstract: Benefiting from recent advances in generative AI and large language models (LLMs), current LLM-driven AI systems are rapidly reshaping how we reason, plan, and make decisions. Yet endowing these systems with human-like temporal intelligence (e.g., understanding and comparing events across time) remains largely unresolved. To address this gap, we introduce a novel Multi-dimensional Hierarchical Temporal Alignment framework (denoted as MHTA), of which the core idea is to effectively ground the temporal alignment of an LLM in both event-specific and cross-event real-world temporal commonsense knowledge. Specifically, we first frame the temporal space as a multi-dimensional hierarchical space, where each dimension comprises its own set of temporal units. Building on this formulation, we curate an initial burn-in dataset in which annotations are constructed to reflect real-world human temporal commonsense in accordance with our defined temporal space. Based on the initial burn-in dataset, we propose two complementary fine-tuning objectives: (i) Grounding the temporal alignment in event-specific temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved through a novel hierarchy-preserving Wasserstein loss, and (ii) Grounding the temporal alignment in cross-event temporal commonsense knowledge, which is achieved via a margin-adaptive triplet loss. To evaluate the effectiveness of MHTA, we conduct extensive experiments on three representative benchmarks (MCTACO, DurationQA, and TimeDial). For example, on the MCTACO dataset, MHTA improves Mistral-7B by 6.0% in accuracy and 10.3% in exact match, and improves DeepSeek-LLM-7B by 5.4% in accuracy and 9.8% in exact match. Combined with different backbones, MHTA surpasses nearly all baselines across the three benchmarks and exceeds the performance of advanced models such as GPT-4o on MCTACO and DurationQA. These results demonstrate that MHTA provides consistent gains in temporal commonsense reasoning across diverse LLM backbones.

title: Predictive distributions driven by sample means, variances and clustering
abstract: Several statistical procedures are based on predictive distributions. Some examples are Bayesian predictive inference, machine learning, species sampling sequences, the prequential approach, causal inference and predictive resampling. This thesis introduces a novel idea for building predictive distributions, where the new datum depends on past observations only through their shape, location and dispersion. A sequence of predictives (beta_n) is proposed, where beta_n depends only on the mean and covariance matrix of past data. Then, beta_n is generalised to another predictive gamma_n, which has a mixture structure based on the clustering of past data. The updating rule of gamma_n is inspired by the Pòlya urns scheme. In addition, gamma_n is used to construct a sequence (r_n) of predictives, which are suitable for regression problems in a Bayesian framework. The beta_n are shown to converge a.s. in total variation to a random law known in closed form. When beta_n is Gaussian, the convergence rate is arbitrarily close to n^{-1/2}. The gamma_n converge in total variation too. Their limit is known explicitly and it has an interesting statistical interpretation. Similar results hold for r_n. Furthermore, the asymptotic behaviour of the copula-based predictive distributions (Hahn et al. 2018) is investigated, as they are a popular predictive model. Sufficient conditions are provided for them to converge in total variation. Various experiments of Bayesian inference via predictive resampling are carried out. It turns out beta_n estimates well population mean and variance, while gamma_n captures also moments of higher order and quantiles. Moreover, gamma_n is compared to two natural competitors: the copula-based predictives and the predictives of Cui and Walker (2024). They all provide precise posterior estimates, but predictive resampling is faster with gamma_n. Finally, r_n is employed for the estimation of regression coefficients. Satisfying outcomes are obtained for different types of data, including non-linear and heteroscedastic ones.

title: Asymptotic properties of k-means and its bias correction for high-dimension, low-sample-size data
abstract: Although k-means is recognized as an effective method for analyzing high-dimension, low-sample-size (HDLSS) data, its asymptotic properties in such contexts remain underexplored. This study aims to deepen the understanding of k-means clustering under practical high-dimensional settings and investigates the asymptotic properties of k-means algorithms in case of HDLSS conditions. Based on the identified asymptotic properties of conventional k-means, a bias-corrected version of k-means was proposed and assessed for performance improvement. Additionally, in line with the current situation that kernel k-means lacks adequate theoretical exploration in high-dimensional environments, a theoretical analysis of kernel kmeans was conducted using a Gaussian kernel function for high-dimensional data, facilitating the theoretical comparison between kernel and standard k-means. Finally, numerical simulations were conducted to demonstrate the effectiveness of both the methods, i.e., the proposed bias-corrected k-means and conventional k-means methods, including kernel k-means, in high-dimensional settings. Practitioners can leverage the bias-corrected k-means for more accurate clustering in high-dimensional contexts, improving data segmentation in fields ranging from bioinformatics to marketing analysis.

title: CChatbot: Secure Lifecycle Management for Persistent Confidential Chatbots
abstract: Chatbots are increasingly deployed in stateful workflows where conversations span multiple sessions maintain persistent conversation state. Protecting such systems requires more than confidential inference: conversation objects must be securely created, processed, stored, resumed, and isolated throughout their lifecycle. This paper presents CChatbot, a TEE-backed confidential chatbot architecture that models conversations as persistent security-sensitive objects governed by an explicit lifecycle. CChatbot combines confidential inference with secure lifecycle management, including ownership enforcement, protected persistence, integrity validation and controlled resumption. We implement CChatbot on an AMD SEV-SNP confidential virtual machine and an NVIDIA H100 confidential GPU. Our evaluation shows that lifecycle management adds only 1.7% overhead over confidential inference while secure create, store and resume operations remain lightweight. On a single-node deployment, CChatbot supports up to 512 concurrent users with affordable interaction latency.

title: Data Processing Inequalities for the Quantum Guesswork
abstract: Quantum guesswork has emerged as a crucial measure in assessing the distinguishability of nonorthogonal quantum states. In this paper, we review and compare previous definitions of the quantum guesswork, and establish the pre and post data processing inequalities (DPIs) that are relevant for the guessing problem. We also derive improved lower and upper bounds on the quantum guesswork in terms of the Shannon entropy and Holevo's information.

title: No Masking Needed: Predicting Latent Semantics for Efficient Pre-training of Encoder-based Language Models
abstract: In this paper, we introduce Latent Semantic Modeling (LSM), a sample-efficient alternative for pre-training encoder-based language models that does not require the use of a special mask symbol. This is beneficial, as it allows us to perform pre-training on naturally occurring sentences (as opposed to such ones that contain an unnatural mask symbol, which symbol is otherwise not included during fine-tuning). The main idea behind LSM is that instead of requiring the language model to return the exact identity of randomly selected (sub)tokens from an input sequence, it determines their latent semantic properties extracted from an auxiliary model using sparse coding over its activations. When fine-tuned for downstream applications, models pre-trained with LSM often perform as good or better as alternatively pre-trained models that use considerably more compute per update steps and which have gone through considerably more pre-training steps, illustrating the improved representation developed during LSM pre-training. We release our code base for replicating our results under https://github.com/szegedai/MLSM.

title: Aspect-Based Sentiment Analysis of Fashion and Apparel Related Reviews using Transformer Model
abstract: The increasing reliance on e-commerce has led to a surge in customer-generated content, making sentiment analysis a crucial tool for understanding consumer preferences. This study presents a novel aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) approach to extract fine-grained insights from customer reviews across multiple product categories, including lingerie, women’s clothing, men’s clothing, kids’ apparel, home & furniture, and flowers & plants. We employ exploratory data analysis (EDA) to uncover key patterns in customer sentiment and utilize a transformer-based model with contrastive learning to enhance sentiment classification accuracy. Our approach effectively captures sentiment variations across nine different aspects, including quality, value for money, style, fit, material, warmth, comfort, support, and how well the product fits. The results demonstrate that our model outperforms traditional sentiment analysis methods, offering a more structured understanding of customer feedback. By analyzing customer sentiments from reviews, businesses can identify dissatisfaction patterns that may contribute to customer churn. Addressing these issues proactively can help improve customer retention and loyalty. These insights can help businesses refine their product offerings and improve customer satisfaction across diverse e-commerce categories.

title: Directional Robustness Asymmetry in Indonesian Sarcasm Detection: A Cross-Platform Evaluation of IndoRoBERTa on X and Reddit
abstract: Sarcasm can reverse sentence polarity, making it one of the hardest problems in natural language processing and a persistent obstacle to reliable sentiment analysis on social media, where models are often deployed on platforms they were not trained on. Research on Indonesian sarcasm has largely stayed within a single domain or tested transfer in only one direction, leaving the cross-domain robustness of the IndoRoBERTa family on the IdSarcasm benchmark unclear. This study measures and compares the cross-domain robustness of IndoRoBERTa-small and IndoRoBERTa-base, with IndoBERT as a baseline, across X (Twitter) and Reddit, using the F1 gap (ΔF1) after cleaning anonymization artifacts, adding a data-size control, and running Stratified 5-Fold cross-validation. The results reveal a one-sided asymmetry: X → Reddit transfer is far more fragile (ΔF1 0.345–0.400) than Reddit → X (0.135–0.240), failing by missing sarcasm (false negatives) rather than over-flagging it (false positives). Practically, training on the context-rich domain (Reddit) and choosing IndoRoBERTa-base give the most reliable cross-platform sarcasm detection, with direction-specific mitigation recommended for robust deployment.

title: ExpEvolve: Structuring and Reusing Experience for Open-Ended Discovery
abstract: Evolutionary coding agents such as AlphaEvolve are one of the notable successes in using Large Language Models (LLMs) to build AI Scientists. These agents tackle open-ended scientific problems by iteratively improving and evolving programs, leveraging the prior knowledge and reasoning capabilities of LLMs. Despite their success, mutations over programs are mostly low-level upon surface heuristics, without a persistent unit of control. In contrast, science compounds through ideas. In this work, we propose ExpEvolve, which injects idea-level extraction and control into evolution: it discovers and leverages the high-level factors from programs that explain scoring differences among different programs. We characterize theoretical conditions on when discovery with idea factors improves sample efficiency. We also build a practical framework to show that the extracted high-level idea factors are helpful for guiding exploitation from experience and exploration when discovery comes to a plateau. Across 11 open-ended mathematical tasks, ExpEvolve significantly improves the final performance and sample efficiency up to 5.0x. The improvements also transfer to 4 other LLMs and to 6 machine learning tasks from MLS-Bench. Analysis shows that ExpEvolve can discover idea-level factors to provide better exploration and exploitation for evolutionary discovery.

title: GenAI use in collaboration
abstract: This dataset supports the study "I Use AI, But I Don't Trust You To: Double Standards in Generative AI Usage in Collaboration." It contains the complete coded survey data collected from a 2×2 between-subject experimental survey administered to 350 participants. The dataset is provided in xlsx format and includes all responses prior to data cleaning, with variables coded according to the accompanying codebook. Measured constructs include participants' perceptions of generative AI's agentic capability and controllability loss, cognitive and emotional distrust toward collaborators who use GenAI, collaboration avoidance intentions, own adoption intention, and control variables. A codebook describing all items and coding schemes is included.

title: TAC-CoT: Tool-Empowered Implicit Chain-of-Thought via Interleaving Explicit Tokens
abstract: LLM-based agentic systems are increasingly combined with CoT reasoning to solve tasks that require accurate reasoning, external knowledge, and multi-step deliberation. Yet, explicit CoT incurs substantial generation overhead, while implicit CoT, which replaces textual rationales with compact continuous tokens, does not naturally support the explicit communication interface required for agentic tool-use. We propose TAC-CoT, a tool-empowered adaptive implicit CoT framework that replaces explicit reasoning traces with compact latent reasoning segments while retaining textual tokens only for tool calls, observations, and final answers. This interleaved design enables agentic tool-use without verbalizing every intermediate reasoning step. Experiments on agentic math and QA benchmarks show that TAC-CoT improves accuracy by up to 8.8 points while reducing model forward passes by up to 6.8x. Furthermore, analyses show that TAC-CoT improves tool-use quality in both single- and multi-tool settings.

title: IMPACTOS DE LA COMPUTACIÓN CUÁNTICA EN LA SEGURIDAD DE SISTEMAS DE VOTACIÓN ELECTRÓNICA
abstract: La tecnología de computación cuántica, con su potencia de cálculo exponencialmente superior a la de las computadoras actuales, hace vulnerables los sistemas críticos, como los sistemas de votación electrónica, lo que significará un riesgo potencial para la integridad de la democracia. Este artículo analiza el impacto de la transición a un sistema de votación cuántica. Al examinar la literatura existente y simular protocolos en un entorno cuántico, el estudio evalúa los beneficios y desafíos relacionados con la seguridad, la integridad y la confiabilidad, con el objetivo de proteger los procesos democráticos contra futuras amenazas tecnológicas.

title: When Does Latent Prediction Error Support Physical Surprise Claims in Video World Models?
abstract: Prediction errors from video world models are often treated as physical surprise, but they can also reflect appearance, static content, motion, or ordinary prediction difficulty. We present an evaluation framework that separates what frozen representations contain, how they organize appearance and physical differences, and what changes a model's own prediction error. On IntPhys2, a benchmark of physically possible and impossible events, we compare representations from latent prediction, masked pixel reconstruction, and simple visual statistics. Appearance remains easy to decode, while V-JEPA2 exposes modest information about whether events are possible or impossible. Looking at the latent geometry, appearance changes become smaller compared with differences between videos, their directions line up more consistently across scenes, and their overlap with physical changes decreases in deeper layers. Across action-conditioned models, incorrect actions raise prediction error, while appearance changes also produce substantial responses. In Physion++ video clips, repeating a single frame can produce higher error than the original clip, while changing color throughout the clip can lower it. Using Kubric, a simulation and rendering framework, we find that impossible events can produce lower error than possible events. A fixed error threshold also incorrectly flags many possible events as impossible. A model can therefore represent physical information and respond to incorrect actions without its native prediction error reliably measuring physical surprise.

title: Just-in-Time Skill Retrieval via Long-Horizon State Tracking
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly rely on external skill libraries to support complex task execution. However, determining which skills are needed remains challenging in long-horizon tasks. Existing methods typically select a fixed skill set before execution, implicitly assuming that a task's procedural requirements can be determined from its initial description. This assumption is restrictive for long-horizon interaction, where new requirements emerge from intermediate observations, execution outcomes, and newly revealed constraints. This motivates just-in-time skill retrieval, which dynamically selects skills as execution unfolds. Just-in-time skill retrieval is promising but challenging: the utility of a skill depends not only on the current context, but also on the evolving task state shaped by prior steps. To this end, we propose JitSkill, a state-grounded framework that addresses this challenge through continuous task-state tracking. By connecting emerging requirements with accumulated task progress, JitSkill provides procedural support throughout execution without treating each retrieval decision independently. Experiments across three agent benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness in improving long-horizon task completion. Our code is available at https://github.com/XMUDeepLIT/JitSkill.git/.

title: Night Jasmine Blooming Optimization (NJBO): A Novel Nature-Inspired Algorithm for Electrical Engineering Applications
abstract: Optimization algorithms have become vital to the solution of complex optimization problems that are difficult to solve using conventional methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithm called the Night Jasmine Blooming Optimization (NJBO) algorithm, which is inspired by the blooming of the night jasmine plant (Cestrum nocturnum). The suggested algorithm combines adaptive hormonal regulation, Gibberellin-based disturbance, scent-guided exploitation, elite preservation, and Nelder–Mead local refinement, which allows us to have a balanced exploration–exploitation process. It was tested with thirteen classical benchmark functions and the CEC2017 benchmark suites and benchmarked with several well-known and recent metaheuristic methods. As a practical application, NJBO was used for identification of an IIR system and optimal design of a five-stage Cockcroft–Walton voltage multiplier circuit. Additionally, the scalability analysis, runtime evaluation, component contribution analysis, parameter sensitivity analysis, and statistical validation with the Friedman ranking test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test were performed to assess the system completely. The results show that NJBO is a very effective general-purpose optimization algorithm with competitive convergence performance, good optimization accuracy, and stability for the benchmark and engineering optimization problems that were investigated.

title: CrossSWE: Benchmarking Cross-Repository Joint Development for Coding Agents
abstract: As coding agents achieve increasingly high success rates on software engineering benchmarks, recent efforts have sought to increase task complexity through longer horizons and more extensive code modifications. However, real-world software development often spans multiple interdependent repositories, introducing additional challenges in dependency reasoning, change propagation, and interface consistency. Rather than further increasing complexity within individual repositories, we introduce CrossSWE, a benchmark for cross-repository joint development comprising 171 real-world instances spanning 165 repositories, 20 technical domains, and 13 programming languages. CrossSWE verifies the necessity of coordinated changes by testing whether partial repository modifications are insufficient to achieve the intended behavior. Our evaluation of five LLMs reveals substantial challenges, with the strongest model, GPT-6.1 Sol, achieving only 58.48% Pass@1. Furthermore, cross-repository inconsistencies emerge as the most prevalent failure mode (44.2%), highlighting the difficulty of maintaining consistency across interdependent repositories.

title: Renormalized Cellular Intelligence: When Does Model Reduction Preserve Collective Capability?
abstract: As multi-agent systems grow in size and complexity, understanding which features of their interactions support collective capability becomes increasingly difficult. Can a simpler description preserve both task performance and the measured contribution of interactions between agents? Preserving collective dynamics alone is insufficient: reduction can alter decision-relevant information or give a non-communicating baseline access to pooled observations, distorting the measured advantage of interaction. We introduce Renormalized Cellular Intelligence (RCI), a framework for specifying and auditing capability preservation across scales. RCI treats the task, interacting dynamics, matched baseline, decision interfaces, and resource budget as a joint object of reduction. It specifies dynamical closure, decision compatibility, and preservation of the intended baseline comparison, and bounds the resulting error in relative capability gain. An exact analytical construction demonstrates task-score preservation, while a counterexample shows how closed reduced dynamics can erase the measured interaction gain. Using cellular systems as models of locally interacting agents, we evaluate three reduction candidates on five frozen learned models without retraining. The final candidate reduces the evolving state from eight to five dimensions per cell (37.5%). title: For SMEs Limited Resources, Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Technology Enhances Customer Relationship Management
abstract: In this rapidly advancing digital era, Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprise (SME) owners are required to adapt to technological changes to remain competitive in the market. One strategy that can be implemented is optimizing Customer Relationship Management (CRM) through the use of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot technology. This paper examines how AI chatbot technology can be an effective solution to improve the quality of CRM for SMEs with limited resources. AI chatbots offer the ability to provide fast, consistent, and personal responses to customers 24/7, collect customer data for preference analysis, and reduce the workload of customer service teams. Despite having various advantages, AI chatbot implementation also faces challenges such as limitations in handling complex cases, initial development costs, and the need to consider customer data privacy. Selecting the right AI chatbot solution, considering the business characteristics of SMEs, is key to the successful implementation of this strategy.

title: From Logs to Faults: Reference-Free Fault Localization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Pipelines
abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines are widely used for domain-specific question answering, yet locating faults remains manual and time-consuming. Fault localization is challenging because RAG pipelines consist of interdependent stages, where faults can propagate downstream, masking their origin, or remain undetected even when the final answer is correct. Existing evaluation approaches often focus on individual stages and rely on reference answers or code instrumentation. We present RAGLog, which detects and localizes faults across RAG stages using execution logs, without requiring reference answers or code instrumentation. RAGLog transforms heterogeneous API logs into a common RAG schema and combines rule-based, embedding-based, and LLM-based checks to identify faulty stages. We introduce a live fault injector and RAGLog Faults, a dataset of 3,134 runs from five RAG pipelines with stage-level fault labels. With Claude Haiku 5.5, RAGLog achieves a pooled F1 score of 0.73 on runs with naturally occurring faults, outperforming Claude Code (0.58) and Codex (0.52), and comparable effectiveness on runs with injected faults (0.84 versus 0.80 and 0.82, respectively). It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.

It analyzes runs in approximately five seconds at US\$0.005 each, with overall lower cost and latency than agent baselines. RAGLog is available as an open-source tool for debugging, evaluating, and monitoring RAG pipelines.

title: Non-Autoregressive and Iterative Refinement Non-Autoregressive Transformer with Additional Graph Layer for Urdu-to-English Machine Translation
abstract: Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved state-of-the-art performance using autoregressive Transformer. However, the trade-off between translation quality and decoding speed remains a central challenge. This problem is further intensified for low-resource languages such as Urdu, where limited parallel data and complex linguistic structure result in poor translation quality and reduced model effectiveness. To overcome this problem Non-Autoregressive Transformer (NAT) and Non-Autoregressive Transformer with Iterative Refinement (iNAT) are proposed. This paper investigates NAT and iNAT for low resource language Urdu-English machine translation. We analyze translation accuracy and their effectiveness for low-resource language pairs. Experimental results show that both NAT and iNAT outperform the baseline Autoregressive Transformer (ART) in terms of translation accuracy. However, the overall translation quality remains limited due to the complex linguistic structure and resource scarcity of the Urdu-English pair. To address this limitation, we further refine these architectures by introducing an additional graph-based learning layer that captures latent relationships among tokens through attention-driven graph representations. The proposed graph-enhanced model learns contextual dependencies by dynamically constructing graphs over attention representations. Experimental evaluation demonstrates that the proposed architecture improves the translation performance of both NAT and iNAT models. On the Urdu-English translation task, the proposed model achieves a 3.0% higher BLEU score than the baseline models. The findings highlight the significance of incorporating graph-based layer to enhance translation quality, making NMT systems more effective for low-resource and linguistically complex languages such as Urdu.

title: Hinted Scaling Laws
abstract: Scaling laws predict the outcome of large, expensive training runs by extrapolating trends from smaller, cheaper runs. On downstream accuracy evaluations, these predictions fail when the weaker models produced by the cheaper runs score near zero accuracy, because these scores give no trend to extrapolate to larger scales. We introduce hinted scaling laws, which use privileged information to turn a benchmark into a continuum of easier versions so that even the small models score above zero. We find that accuracy rises smoothly and predictably with the hint level, enabling new types of scaling laws that operate below the noise threshold. On the Delphi pretraining ladder, a hinted scaling law fit on models trained with at most 10^{20} FLOPs forecasts the GSM8K accuracy of a 10^{23} FLOP model (25.9%) to within 3 percentage points; a standard scaling law under-forecasts it by 13 percentage points when fit on the same models and by 12 even with models up to 10^{22} FLOPs in the fit. Across both this pretraining ladder and a collection of post-trained model families, hinted scaling laws reduce the median forecasting error on GSM8K, AIME and HLE from 21 percentage points to 4.3. Hinting also reduces the number of test examples needed to tell whether one model is better than another by widening the accuracy gaps between models while approximately preserving their order: a single hinted rollout per problem ranks nearly indistinguishable models as accurately as five unhinted rollouts. Our results suggest that hinting is a general primitive for improving the accuracy and cost of downstream scaling laws and other prediction tasks in model development.

title: SwahiliAI: Building an Open-Source Artificial Intelligence Ecosystem for East African Languages
abstract: SwahiliAI is a 24-month research proposal to build an open-source AI ecosystem for Swahili and East African languages. Building on existing African NLP work (Masakhane, IrokoBench, UlizaLlama), the project will (i) create openly licensed, domain-specific Swahili instruction data; (ii) fine-tune open-weight large language models with LoRA/QLoRA; (iii) release SwahiliBench-D, an evaluation suite measuring both accuracy and safety; and (iv) pilot applications on Web, SMS and USSD. The first phase focuses on healthcare, agriculture and education, with extensions to financial inclusion, legal aid and employment. Principal researcher: Rodgers Ochieng Oduor (SPRINTER, Nairobi), in collaboration with Dr. Ibrahim Tirimba Ondabu, KCA University.

title: Can AI Reviewers See Your Efforts to Improve Your Paper? A Large-Scale Study of Paper Revision Trajectories
abstract: AI reviewers are increasingly used to assess scientific manuscripts, yet it remains unclear whether their judgments reflect the improvements authors make through revision. We investigate this question using PaperTrajectory-2026, the 2026 release of PaperTrajectory, a dataset of 6,959 paper trajectories across five AI conferences, with automatic annotations of changes along 14 dimensions and separate judgments of overall quality. The annotations show that major improvements emphasize empirical evidence and framing, while later revisions tend toward incremental improvement. Using independent assessments of manuscript versions from eight AI reviewers, we examine whether annotated major improvements receive higher scores, which revision dimensions are associated with score changes, and whether user opinions can outweigh observed revision gains. Every reviewer leaves scores unchanged on most major improvements, and agreement on the direction of score changes is weak. Revision dimensions show some reviewer-specific associations with score increases, but provide limited predictive discrimination and no consistent guide across reviewers. Even when a revision earns a higher neutral score, a brief negative user opinion can erase or reverse that advantage, with substantial variation across reviewers. These findings show that substantive revisions are not consistently reflected in review scores and that observed scoring gains can be vulnerable to user framing, motivating assessments that connect manuscript evidence to overall judgments and remain stable when no scientific evidence changes.

title: Formal verification of bubble sort algorithms in Rocq: correctness, complexity, and stability — Research Artifact
abstract: This artifact by Dmitry V. Alexandrov, Alena Novikova, and Julia Kadeikina accompanies the paper “Formal Verification of Bubble Sort Algorithms in Rocq: Correctness, Complexity, and Stability.” It contains a self-contained Rocq formalization of several functional bubble-sort variants: a well-founded implementation, an instrumented version counting comparisons and swaps, an optimized version with early termination, and a stable version over key–identifier pairs. Machine-checked proofs establish permutation preservation and sortedness, equivalence between the well-founded and instrumented implementations, exact comparison counts, swap–inversion laws, worst-case results, and the best-case behavior of the optimized variant. They also establish an exact comparison formula based on the number of passes performed, as well as the correctness, stability, and agreement with the numeric model of the pair-based implementation. The artifact includes OCaml extraction and executable tests. It requires Rocq 9.1 or later. Use `make check` to verify the proofs and `make test` to run extraction and tests; the latter additionally requires OCaml with `ocamlfind`. All reported assumption checks are closed under the global context. Extracted natural numbers use machine-width OCaml integers, so arithmetic overflow is possible for extremely large inputs or counters.

title: Decision Models as Policy Gates for Coding Agents: Explicit Policy Boundaries Improve Detection and Reduce False Alarms
abstract: Coding agents can destroy data, leak secrets and message the wrong person faster than a human can review. Could a decision model catch these risks at runtime? We evaluated 22 hosted decision models and two prompted general models as classifiers for a multi-rule policy engine. A synthetic dataset of 2,643 tool calls was labeled blind against 28 rules, with a sealed holdout. With a single shared preamble in both conditions, explicit boundaries written as examples and counterexamples raised recall by 5.5-26.1 percentage points on all 23 available models and reduced false positives on 21. Jev 1.14's recall rose from 89.3% to 98.2%, while unnecessary interruptions fell from 30.6% to 4.8% of 252 clean actions. With examples, its median latency was 120 ms at $0.46 per thousand requests. Strong models retained the recall gains when concrete names were replaced by generic descriptions; three largely retained them when the same boundaries were written as prose. On 16 new scenarios written after the initial studies, a follow-up improved recall on 22 of 23 models and reduced unnecessary interruptions on 21. We release the dataset, rule texts and harness.

title: Defeating Quantum Obfuscation in Adversarial AI Distillation: Bell-State Monogamy Traps, Non-Commutative Berry Phase Reasoning Graphs, and KKT-Grover Resonance Amplifiers over the 64-Bit Goldilocks Field
abstract: As fault-tolerant quantum computing (Q-Day) enables Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) weight-space inversion to audit illicitly distilled artificial intelligence models, sophisticated adversaries have formulated "Counter-Scenario A: Quantum Obfuscation"—deploying Quantum Machine Learning (QML) unitary scrambling and intentional noise entanglement to conceal stolen training signatures and obstruct KKT stationarity reconstruction. This monograph proves via quantum information theory, differential geometry, and algebraic cryptography that any adversarial manipulation of quantum entanglement or unitary noise injection to mask intellectual property (IP) theft inevitably generates an unforgeable physical-layer forensic signature. We formalize three active quantum honeypot countermeasures: (1) the Bell-State Monogamy Trap, exploiting the Coffman–Kundu–Wootters (CKW) monogamy of entanglement inequality ($\tau_{AB} + \tau_{AE} \le \tau_{A(BE)}$) so that entangling external obfuscation noise $E$ with distilled API trajectories forces a deterministic collapse of pre-entangled Bell-pair correlations and an observable von Neumann entropy spike; (2) the Topological Berry Phase Reasoning Graph, embedding non-commutative operator algebras ($[\hat{A}, \hat{B}] \neq 0$) into multi-step Chain-of-Thought (CoT) deduction paths that accumulate a gauge-invariant geometric Berry phase ($\gamma_{\text{Berry}} = \oint_{\mathcal{C}} \mathcal{A}_{\mu} dR^{\mu} \not\equiv 0$) under adversarial unitary obfuscation; and (3) the KKT Margin Resonance Amplifier (Grover's Resonance Trap), seeding singular margin gradients that constructively interfere with Grover diffusion operators to exponentially amplify stolen dual KKT multipliers ($\lambda_{\text{trap}} \to 1$). Finally, we integrate these three traps with deterministic verification over the 64-bit Goldilocks prime field ($\mathbb{F}_p, p = 2^{64} - 2^{32} + 1$) inside QFS-zkVM, RTO P2.0, Q-SAFA, and title: HaloGuard 2.0: An Open-Weights Constitutional Output Guard for Multilingual Response Safety
abstract: An input guard decides whether a request reaches the model, but never sees what the model says. Harm that emerges during generation, because a jailbreak passed the input layer or a benign request drifted into operational detail, is visible only on the output side and only as tokens arrive. We present HaloGuard 2.0, an open-weight streaming output guard that assigns a safe/unsafe probability to every response token in a single forward pass, so a deployment can stop the stream once harm is confirmed. The guard reuses the constitution of HaloGuard 1.0, our input guard, to organise a 478,532-response training corpus, and supervises each token from the point where the response becomes harmful. We find that a guard trained on conventionally shaped data learns a shortcut specific to streaming: it judges the prompt instead of the response, and handles only 13.9% of matched safe/unsafe response pairs correctly. We correct this with a second phase on 106,043 counterfactual responses built around the base guard's own failure modes, and release the equal-weight average of the base and corrective models. On six English response-safety benchmarks, HaloGuard 2.0-0.8B reaches a macro F1 of 83.6 (83.3 on held-out halves of the decision-rule search), up from 72.8, with 38% fewer false positives. It matches the strongest full-response guards with 5-10x fewer parameters and is 2.6 points above the strongest streaming guard, Qwen3Guard-Stream-4B. A multilingual variant, HaloGuard 2.0-Poly-0.8B, trained on PolyGuardMix, reaches 83.1 F1 on the response labels of PolyGuardPrompts across 17 languages, 5.0 points above the strongest baseline. On one H100 the guard costs 0.37 ms per token per stream when moderating 64 concurrent responses. Both guards are hardened continuously through the weekly red-teaming protocol of HaloGuard 1.0, extended here to the output layer.

title: Three specified routes to a hidden battery need stopped at feasibility: a pre-registered null on open LLMs run on one 32 GB Mac
abstract: A bounded feasibility report on three specified routes toward hidden battery-need signals in open language models on one 32 GB Mac. Direct answer-token steering did not pass the complete specificity rule; thinking-route interpretation was limited by an unvalidated leak instrument; a downstream trained-receptor design stopped at task qualification. Saved-score paired intervals retain a small positive hidden log-odds contrast alongside a larger text-associated rise. The archive contains scoped protocols, code, saved scores and portable offline checks; it does not establish impossibility of hidden need states or a clean hidden mechanism.

title: FOLLIE: Automated Reasoning over the First Dataset of Sentences with their First-Order Logical Representation for French
abstract: FOLLIE (for First-Order Logic for Language Inference and Entailment for French) connects French sentences, compositional first-order representations and automated natural language inference (NLI). The first French NLI-ready, NL-to-FOL resource, it contains 19,983 inference records and 36,987 non-empty sentence-slot--formula mappings from six heterogeneous NLI sources, retaining French lexical material and source problem structure. Its silver annotations are produced by a neural--symbolic pipeline, with 111 separately identified LLM-assisted additions. The construction combines morphosyntactic analysis, probability-conditioned categorial multitagging, grammatical proof search, discourse representation and first-order semantic construction. Stage-wise experiments show substantial gains in derivation coverage; analyses of conjunction distributions, logical-operator incidence and scope alternation characterise the resulting resource. We then develop an automatic inference engine whose input-conditioned background theories address lexical relations, quantification, quantities, event structure and temporal dependencies. Prover9 supplies proofs for entailment and contradiction, while Mace4 supports bounded consistency checks. Three-way accuracies are 65.37% on all 335 FraCaS-FR problems, 70.33% on 300 GQNLI-FR problems and 71.35% on 9,399 eligible SICK-FR records pooled across splits. Agreement with reference labels among committed decisions is 93.53%, 100.00% and 98.66%, at commitment coverage of 41.49%, 37.00% and 15.05%, respectively. Worked constructions, axiom schemas and proof analyses explain these outcomes and identify the contributions of scope, reference, lexical knowledge and numerical structure. FOLLIE provides a French experimental basis for studying the representations and assumptions that connect sentence interpretation to deductive inference.

title: Pre-registration of a replication of the inference-latency claims of REVBRAIN (arXiv 2610.38558)
abstract: Frozen pre-registration (1 Nov 2026) of a private replication of two quantitative claims of arXiv 2610.38558 (Pankka, Lehtinen, Roine): that the median inference latency of the autoregressive WaveNet baseline is about 52x that of REVBRAIN at 1 sample per input and about 3170x at 100 samples per input, using the authors' released latency script (repo hpankka/revbrain, commit 4418b775) on one Kaggle T4 GPU. Bounds are half the paper's ratios (26 and 1585); 10 invocation pairs; percentile bootstrap. Contains the decision code, harness, power simulation, planted-effect table and the run kernel. Deposited before the main run. Outcome wording: Replicated / Did not replicate / Inconclusive under protocol X.

title: Order-Only On-Policy Distillation
abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own generations by matching the teacher's token probabilities. These probabilities entangle two kinds of information: which tokens the teacher prefers, and how confident it is. The latter reflects the teacher's own capacity and calibration, which a smaller student may be unable to reproduce. Because the teacher temperature changes these values without changing the ordering, OPD is also sensitive to the temperature choice. We ask whether the teacher's ordering of candidate tokens is enough, and propose Order-Only On-Policy Distillation (O^{3}PD). At each student-generated prefix, O^{3}PD trains the student to reproduce the order of the teacher's top-K tokens, without fitting their probability values. The objective is therefore invariant to the teacher temperature and needs no temperature tuning. Across six teacher--student pairs, O^{3}PD outperforms OPD on the average over HMMT25, AIME24, and AIME25 in every pair, by up to 2.9 points, with gains of up to 5.6 points on AIME25. Other ranking losses yield similar gains, so the benefit comes from ordinal supervision itself. Analysis shows that O^{3}PD departs further from the teacher's probabilities than OPD, yet reproduces its ranking more faithfully and yields a stronger student. The ranking, not the probability values, thus carries the knowledge that on-policy distillation needs to transfer.

title: Cumulative Stabilization Probabilities During PPO Learning: A Paired Reward Study for Cart-Pendulum Swing-Up
abstract: This simulation study investigates how the cumulative probability of successful cart–pendulum swing-up and sustained stabilization changes with training progress and physical evaluation time. The target quantity, H(g,t), measures the probability that a controller has completed its first qualifying stabilization interval by time t at training generation g. Two reward formulations are compared using 100 paired training seeds, 1,000 PPO rollout/update generations per controller, and full 20-second evaluations every ten generations. The simulator uses fully nonlinear uniform-rod dynamics. Success requires a simultaneous two-second hold within specified cart-position, cart-velocity, upright-angle and angular-velocity tolerances. At the final generation, 68/100 bounded-reward controllers and 52/100 quadratic-reward controllers succeeded by 20 seconds. The observed paired difference was 16 percentage points, with a conservative 95% interval of −3.461 to +34.184 points. Quadratic achieved substantial success earlier during training but subsequently regressed. Final completion-time curves crossed, showing that neither reward uniformly dominated. The comparison is a follow-up using an already observed bounded-reward reference arm. Failures, censoring and learning regressions are retained. Supporting material provides event data, source code, configurations and reproducible analysis.

title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
abstract: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

title: A Detector Score Is Not a Release Risk: What PII Detection Benchmarks Certify About Deployment, Why 'Rivals Human Annotators' and 'Fails Under Shift' Are Both Measured, and the Coverage Audit a Release Decision Needs
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Automatic detection of personally identifiable information (PII) is the step that decides what text may leave an organisation, and its published record appears to contradict itself. Clinical de-identification systems have been reported to match or exceed human annotators, with recall above 0.94 on held-out notes and above 0.99 for one rule-based tool; a 2026 stress test reports that encoder, rule-based and language-model detectors all degrade under noisy and informal input, with location recall falling below 0.5, and a unified benchmark reports span F1 below 0.14 for every system it tried. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that most of the contradiction is in what the scores index rather than in the detectors. A PII detection score carries four indices that headlines omit: how the test text relates to the text the detector was built on, the scoring rule, the taxonomy that defines what counts, and the unit over which misses are aggregated. The same shared-task system misses 9.1 percent of protected items under one official rule and 3.6 percent under another; the lowest unified-benchmark scores come partly from entity types the evaluated detectors do not define; and in the 2026 stress test several of the losses attributed to the language model are spans it covered under another label. A residual shift effect survives every index: under fixed scoring, cross-institution transfer cost about ten points of strict F1, and systems run unmodified on new psychiatric records scored a median of 0.63. None of the indices is the quantity a release decision needs, which is the probability that a released document still carries an identifying item someone could find. The paper consolidates the evidence in a table, derives how per-item recall compounds at the document level, and gives a coverage-audit procedure with the sample sizes a release claim requires.

A PII detection score carries four indices that headlines omit: how the test text relates to the text the detector was built on, the scoring rule, the taxonomy that defines what counts, and the unit over which misses are aggregated. The same shared-task system misses 9.1 percent of protected items under one official rule and 3.6 percent under another; the lowest unified-benchmark scores come partly from entity types the evaluated detectors do not define; and in the 2026 stress test several of the losses attributed to the language model are spans it covered under another label. A residual shift effect survives every index: under fixed scoring, cross-institution transfer cost about ten points of strict F1, and systems run unmodified on new psychiatric records scored a median of 0.63. None of the indices is the quantity a release decision needs, which is the probability that a released document still carries an identifying item someone could find. The paper consolidates the evidence in a table, derives how per-item recall compounds at the document level, and gives a coverage-audit procedure with the sample sizes a release claim requires.

title: EarthJev: Calibrated, Non-Generative Answers to Natural-Language Questions about Sentinel-2 Land Cover
abstract: Vision-language models for remote sensing answer questions about satellite images by generating text: every answer costs a decoding loop, has to be parsed back to an option, and comes without a usable probability. We present EarthJev, a 0.8B-parameter model that answers typed questions about multispectral Sentinel-2 patches without generating any token. All 12 bands enter the vision encoder of Qwen3.5-0.8B through a widened input layer initialised from the RGB kernels, and, following the open OneJev recipe, the answer is read from the logits of the option letters at a single position and trained with cross-entropy plus Brier score. Under a pre-specified analysis plan, we compare it with the same backbone fine-tuned to generate the answer and with three multimodal language models fine-tuned with LoRA, all trained on the same 70,890 questions from 5% of BigEarthNet v2.0 and timed in one job on the same GPU; VQA models that classify over a fixed answer vocabulary are reported as a reference for the cost of answering only the questions seen in training. EarthJev answers a question in 19.9 ms, 4.3 to 8.7 times faster than the multimodal language models and 6.8 times faster than its own backbone used generatively; when all the questions about an image are asked together, it answers them in 42.8 ms, 3.7 to 10.1 times faster than the batched generative models. On 36,028 test questions it reaches 86.0% accuracy (three seeds), 0.6 and 1.2 points below the two 2B multimodal models and 3.5 points below the remote-sensing EarthDial-4B, with answers that are valid by construction and calibrated probabilities (ECE 0.006). Replacing the nine non-RGB bands with their mean costs 4.5 points, so the model uses the multispectral input, and in an ablation training the whole vision encoder raises accuracy to 88.4% at the same cost. Code and model: https://github.com/CosmoIknosLab/EarthJev

title: The AI Agentic Architect Workbook: A Practical Companion: Foundations, Skills, and Governance Drills
abstract: The free companion workbook to Becoming an Agentic Architect: Designing Agentic Systems You Can Approve, Govern, and Defend (https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0HPY1RZ2C). More than 160 practice drills, each with a worked example and an at-a-glance figure, help non-coders who approve and oversee AI agents turn the book’s seven-stage spine and its GAMUT framework (Goal, Autonomy, Memory, Uncertainty, Tools) into habits, working against real, published cases and ending in a full Capstone exercise. Available as PDF and EPUB.

title: ParetoSaddler: Pareto-Guided Optimization of Agent Harnesses for Quality and Cost
abstract: Harness optimization can substantially improve LLM agents without modifying model weights, but existing methods primarily optimize response quality. Extending them to joint quality--cost optimization introduces a challenge: applying the deployment preference during intermediate updates can prematurely reject candidates that are valuable for later improvements. We introduce ParetoSaddler, which addresses this mismatch by separating intermediate candidate promotion from final deployment selection. At each iteration, an optimizer updates a parent harness to produce a candidate, and then compares the two over repeated executions and uses Bayesian bootstrap Pareto support to promote candidates showing credible progress in either quality or cost. Promoted candidates receive broader development evaluation and remain available as parents for later optimization steps. We evaluate ParetoSaddler on ClawMark and GAIA2 using domain-disjoint splits. On ClawMark, ParetoSaddler improves quality from 70.86\% to 81.35\% while reducing cost from \1.17 to 1.01 per task; on GAIA2, it improves quality from 56.22\% to 62.89\% while reducing cost from \0.78 to 0.45 per task. The Pareto-selected harnesses also achieve higher quality at lower cost than quality-only harness optimization. Analysis shows that Pareto-aware optimization retains intermediate candidates that would be discarded by deployment preference but can support later improvements, while Bayesian bootstrap screening filters out candidates whose gains are weakly supported across runs.

title: Data for "Can Large Language Models Review the Scientific Literature? A Test Against a 102-Article Benchmark"
abstract: Data, prompts, raw tool outputs and figure data for a study testing whether AI tools can carry out the steps of a scientific literature review, against a published, manually constructed review of the Spanish plume literature (102 articles; Schultz et al. 2025, Monthly Weather Review). The study covers four steps: finding the articles, interpreting them, synthesizing across them, and proposing future work. Each experiment folder holds its locked prompt, the original tool outputs, and clean per-article tables. Publisher-hosted article PDFs and the benchmark's full database are not included.

title: Decoupled Predictive Decision Making: A Shared Conditional Predictor for Agents
abstract: Agent decisions depend on empirical relationships that deployment observations reveal and task descriptions alone may leave unresolved. We introduce Decoupled Predictive Decision Making (DPDM), an architecture that formulates heterogeneous agent decisions as conditional prediction with a shared pretrained learner. Language models provide semantic representations of current and historical records, while a general-purpose conditional predictor predicts task-defined targets from the represented evidence. Pretraining supplies reusable inference capability; deployment evidence instantiates problem-specific predictions without updating either model's neural parameters. Tool judgments, candidate preferences, and reasoning assessments share an evidence-and-query interface, with predictions mapped to choices by a decision rule. This architecture establishes complementary sources of agent capability: semantic knowledge acquired through language pretraining and empirical inference acquired through structured-data pretraining. A single frozen LimiX-2 predictor serves all five task categories. With Qwen3.5-27B as the semantic encoder, DPDM raises mean accuracy across 50 benchmarks from 78.80% with few-shot prompting to 84.92% under their respective evaluated history budgets, and reaches 82.33% with identical histories and queries. On ToolPRMBench's BFCL and ToolSandbox tasks, absolute accuracy gains are 34.26% and 28.87%, respectively, at the methods' respective evaluated history budgets. Accuracy improves as history grows. With identical imbalanced histories, mean balanced accuracy improves by an absolute 14.51% across five reasoning-step assessment tasks and four encoders. DPDM makes learning from experience an independently improvable foundation-model capability, creating a shared route for advances in conditional prediction to improve decisions across agent tasks.

title: 层门控:从零训练与预训练后训练的两组结果(待复核)
abstract: 执行器工程第四篇(合集第九篇)。汇总本系列层门控实验的两族对照:(一)从零训练:小模型 1.2M(3/6 层,代价≈0)、GPT-2 small 124M 1MB(5.3/12 层,+6.8%)、GPT-2 small 124M 100MB(5.8/12 层,+2.7%)、Qwen2.5-1.5B 100MB(12.3/28 层,+1.1%);(二)预训练 + LoRA 后训练:Qwen2.5-7B(28 层,LoRA r=16,1MB,2000 步,目标 26/24/22 层)——层数没有压下来(best 仍 91.8%/85.8%/79.5%),PPL 没有降反升(7.01 → 9.71/12.93/12.79,+38%~+85%),目标 26 组后段门控塌缩(PPL 1243)。结论:从零训练时层门控在 1.2M~1.5B 规模上都便宜;预训练 + 轻量后训练 + 小数据不行;关键变量是训练方式而非参数量。单种子为主、数据有限、仅 PPL,结论保守,不声称新方法。(3B 预训练+LoRA 组结果与 7B 同类,未单列以避免重复。)

title: SWE-Trail: History-Guided Trajectory Collection for Coding Agent Training
abstract: Coding agents solve repository issues through long sequences of exploration, editing, and validation. These trajectories are increasingly used as post-training data, so how they are collected shapes what the trained model learns. A common approach is to sample multiple trajectories independently for each issue and then select or curate them. However, as more trajectories are sampled independently, later trajectories become increasingly redundant, even though earlier trajectories could guide where subsequent collection effort should be spent. A natural way to use this history is to expose it to the coding agent as advice. But training on such trajectories can make the model rely on advice that is unavailable at test time, creating a train-test mismatch. Instead, we argue that history should guide where collection effort is spent, while the coding agent decides what to generate. We introduce SWE-Trail, a trajectory collector that uses earlier trajectories to guide subsequent collection while keeping that history outside the coding agent's context. During a new rollout, SWE-Trail uses history to identify a state where additional collection effort may be useful. There, the coding agent proposes candidate next actions from its ordinary context, and SWE-Trail briefly executes them from the same checkpoint to decide which route continues. We evaluate collection approaches by training student models on the trajectories they produce. For a 124B student initialized from Ling-3.0-flash-base, SWE-Trail improves mean resolution over independent sampling by 2.33 and 1.60 percentage points on SWE-bench Multilingual and SWE-bench Pro, respectively. Without history, the same pipeline produces more resolved trajectories than independent sampling, but improves by only 0.11 points on Multilingual. These results show the value of using history to guide collection without exposing it to the coding agent.

title: ALE semantic interoperability experiments (E1–E7): code, ontology, synthetic test data and aggregated results
abstract: Replication package for the book chapter Semantic Interoperability of Heterogeneous RDF-Based Knowledge Models: Expressiveness Assessment, Loss-Aware Mapping and Integration in an Agricultural Advisory Environment by J. Rogushina, A. Gladun, S. Pryima, O. Anishchenko and A. Savochka (under review for Advanced Computing Applications, Springer). The package contains: the programs of experiments E1–E7: mapping of OWL 2 ontologies to Semantic MediaWiki (direct mapping M0 and loss-aware mapping M1) and back, competency questions, n-ary registered uses of plant protection products, personalised projections, construction of LLM context from the knowledge graph (S2) with answer control (G2), evaluation with real LLMs (llama3.1:8b, gemma3:4b) against BM25, dense and hybrid retrieval baselines, and Semantic MediaWiki scalability; the working draft of the ALE ontology (1.0.0-draft) used in the experiments, with synthetic test individuals and SPARQL competency questions; open data of the State Register of pesticides and agrochemicals of Ukraine (2008–2024), redistributed unchanged; aggregated results and figures. Records extracted from the copyrighted handbook «Пестициди» (2019) are not included. The package contains the extraction programs and SHA-256 checksums, so these data can be regenerated and verified from one's own copy of the handbook. Synthetic data are marked as such. See README.md. Licences: code GPL-2.0-or-later; ontology and data derived from it CC BY-SA 4.0; other results and documentation CC BY 4.0; register data — open data of the Ministry of Economy of Ukraine (see LICENSES.md). The published ALE ontology, version 1.0.0, is a separate record: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23643625. Funding: Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine, research project "Development of an Intelligent Support Environment for Agricultural Advisory Services Based on the Integration of Semantic Wiki Technologies and Artificial Intelligence" (state registration No. 0126U000765).

title: Switch-SWE: Do Coding Agents Hold Focus When Switching Between Unfinished Tasks?
abstract: Software development sessions often involve several unfinished tasks rather than one issue carried through to completion. As coding agents take on repository-level development, they need to recover an earlier task's requirements and partial progress after intervening work. Existing repository-level benchmarks typically score one issue-to-patch episode and do not directly measure whether an agent can resume a task after advancing other unfinished work in the same repository. We introduce \ourmethod, a benchmark for focus-task resumption in sessions that interleave unfinished tasks drawn from the same source repository, with a persistent checkout for each task. Each focus task is evaluated in matched uninterrupted and switched sessions with identical focus requirements and executable verifiers. The switched session interleaves ordered stages from other unfinished tasks in the same repository, while only the final focus patch is scored. \ourmethod~contains 200 focus tasks from 19 Python repositories, reconstructed from issue, pull-request, and review histories and rendered as 400 matched session specifications. Across 7 coding agents, interleaved unfinished work produces an average focus-task resolution gap of 11.5 percentage points, ranging from 6.0 to 15.0 percentage points. Trajectory analysis identifies cross-task requirement confusion and loss of task state as recurrent resumption behaviors. We introduce a plug-in context-management module that selects task-relevant history and maintains concise task-state summaries. On OpenCode, the module improves focus-task completion under same-repository task switching by 5.5 to 15.5 percentage points across the evaluated models. Code is available at github.com/Miraclecsc/Switch-SWE.

title: Watermark shortcuts in speech deepfake detection: code and results
abstract: Code and result files for the paper "Watermark shortcuts in speech deepfake detection: Framing, mitigation and explanation faithfulness". The study trains spoofing countermeasures (frozen XLS-R and WavLM, fine-tuned XLS-R, and a LoRA-adapted Qwen2.5-Omni-3B audio language model) on ASVspoof 2019 LA with spoofs carrying one of four open-source watermarks (AudioSeal, PerTh, SilentCipher, WavMark), and measures framing of watermarked genuine speech, fix transfer, label-blind augmentation, a representation-based risk score, and the faithfulness of the audio language model's explanations. The code archive contains the experiment scripts, and scripts that recompute every table and figure of the paper from the result archive. The result archive contains exactly the files the paper was computed from, with a README and SHA-256 checksums. Speech audio is not redistributed: ASVspoof 2019 LA (doi:10.7488/ds/2555) and In-the-Wild are available from their distributors, and the watermarked copies can be regenerated with the code.

title: MedPsy: State-of-the-Art Small Medical Language Models for Efficient Edge Deployment
abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. Reasoning models that fit edge memory budgets can produce long reasoning traces, increasing sequential decoding, end-to-end latency, energy consumption, and KV-cache memory pressure. We present MedPsy, a family of text-only 1.7B and 4B medical language models designed for edge deployment, targeting this accuracy-generation-efficiency trade-off. Our recipe combines a synthetic medical data pipeline over biology, medicine, and health seeds with chain-of-thought targets from a 235B medical-focused LLM teacher; a four-stage post-training curriculum comprising two SFT stages followed by two RL stages with hard-sample mining; and an edge deployment evaluation spanning multiple GGUF quantization variants and real-device inference on laptop and smartphone hardware. On seven closed-ended medical benchmarks, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-1.5-4B by 19.34 points and matches MedGemma-27B while being 6.75x smaller; MedPsy-1.7B outperforms MedGemma-1.5-4B by 11.42 points despite being less than half its size. On HealthBench-Hard, MedPsy-4B surpasses MedGemma-27B by 15.33 points, while MedPsy-1.7B surpasses it by 11.66 points despite being ~16x smaller. evidence.abstract: Medical language models promise expert clinical support, but the strongest open-source LLMs remain too large for private edge-device deployment, while compact medical models still trail substantially on knowledge-intensive and real-world healthcare tasks. title: The effects of dataset size and search frequency on the computational efficiency of linear and binary search
abstract: As datasets grow, the cost of retrieving information becomes increasingly important. This study aims to understand how data size and search frequency affect the comparison counts and execution times of linear and binary search, while also considering the costs of sorting and maintaining ordered data. A Python program compared datasets of 100, 1,000, 10,000, and 1,000,000 elements at search frequencies of 1, 10, 100, and 1,000 searches. Linear search was applied to shuffled datasets, whereas binary search was applied to sorted datasets. For the 1,000,000-element dataset at a frequency of 1,000, the mean comparison count per search was 496,944.9864 for linear search and 18.9492 for binary search, representing a 99.9962% reduction in comparisons with binary search, averaged across 1,000 searches. The reported mean time to insert an element into a sorted Python list increased to approximately 0.116 seconds at 1,000,000 elements. The results illustrated the distinction between search costs on prepared data and the additional costs of sorting or maintaining sorted order. The reported search-time values are retained at their stated precision; their scope (per-search means or batch totals) must be identified before total-runtime conclusions can be finalized. The study relates these findings to the broader use of database indexes.
